description: Cluster 1 consists of 373 JBIM articles related to business networks. This cluster is the largest and also has the highest number of cited publications contributed by 325 corresponding authors. The cluster occupies the third-highest rank for total citations (TC: 5,733). The collaboration matrices suggest that 301 articles in the cluster are primarily co-authored. The cluster produced the highest number of articles in each active year (PAY: 14.35) of the 26 years of JBIM. Such indications signify the prominence of the cluster in terms of activeness and the influence of the cluster’s theme in the journal and the B2B scientific community. The temporal evolution shows that this cluster first appeared in 1992; however, up until 2000, it had only 15 articles. From 2000 onward, the cluster shows continuous growth in productivity. Approximately 70% of the articles in this cluster were published in the past decade. This suggests that Cluster 1 is the fastest-growing theme in the current years of the journal, which makes ‘business networks’ one the most worthwhile avenues for future research. The most discussed themes in the cluster include the topics ‘networks in business markets,’ ‘social capital,’ ‘network competence,’ ‘network location,’ ‘network approach,’ ‘industrial networks,’ ‘network mobilizer,’ ‘supply network integration,’ ‘interorganizational network,’ ‘coordination in innovation,’ ‘network of exchange relationships,’ ‘innovation performance’ and ‘interactive network branding.’ The most influential articles of the cluster are those of Turnbull et al. (1996), Vargo (2009) and Gebauer and Friedli (2005).

Cluster 2 is the second-largest cluster in terms of productivity (TP: 317) and the largest cluster in terms of influence (TC: 7,932). This cluster provides the highest number of citations to JBIM. The cluster broadly discusses customer satisfaction, support and branding. The articles under this theme are credited with the highest average citations (C/P: 25.02; C/CP: 26.18). The cluster consists of 13 articles carrying more than 100 citations and 36 articles carrying more than 50 citations. This indicates that ‘customer satisfaction,’ ‘customer support’ and ‘branding’ are highly influential and prominent themes in the discipline of B2B and industrial marketing. Among all five clusters, Cluster 2 has appeared the most since the inception of the journal. Of the articles, 31 were published between 1986 and 1990, and 14 between 1991 and 1995. The cluster shows no major shift in terms of publications. On average, the cluster carries 45 publications in each of the periods. This reflects the consistency and prominence of the themes from the inception of the journal to 2019. Under the wide umbrella of ‘customer satisfaction, support and branding,’ the major topics covered include ‘customer perceived value,’ ‘customer satisfaction,’ ‘service support,’ ‘decision-support system,’ ‘value co-creation,’ ‘B2B value exchange,’ ‘service evaluation,’ ‘B2B buying process,’ ‘brand management,’ ‘brand image,’ ‘branding implications’ and ‘brand equity.’ The most influential works in this cluster are the studies of Eggert and Ulaga (2002), Grönroos (2004), and Mathieu (2001).

Cluster 3 is the third-largest cluster, with 261 publications submitted by 234 authors and credits 5,825 citations to JBIM. The cluster has been active for 27 years, with a productivity (PAY) of 9.67 and a citation score (CAY) of 215.74 for each active year. Six articles credit at least 100 citations to the journal, and 28 at least 50 citations. As Figure 5 shows, the cluster emerged between 1986 and 1990 with seven publications and substantially grew between 1991 and 1995 with 24 articles. The publication count in the cluster shows a continuously increasing trend among all seven periods. This is a clear indication of the increasing importance of the cluster’s theme for B2B and industrial marketing researchers. It also suggests an area for future research and development. The key areas of discussion under this cluster include ‘business relationships,’ ‘marketing service relationships,’ ‘relationship marketing theory,’ ‘competitor relationship,’ ‘customer relationships,’ ‘marketing communication,’ ‘buyer–seller relationships,’ ‘channel relationships,’ ‘relationship structures,’ ‘relationship,’ ‘marketing relationship quality’ and ‘commitment.’ The articles of Bengtsson and Kock (1999), Wetzels et al. (1998) and Kleinaltenkamp et al. (2006) are the most cited in this cluster.

Cluster 4 consists of 224 JBIM articles focused on knowledge management and innovation. These articles were submitted by 201 authors (NLA: 201), and 204 articles have received citations (NCA: 204). The cluster credits 4,258 citations to the journal, and the average citation per publication is 19.01 (TC: 4258; C/P: 19.01). The cluster has actively published for 30 years (NAY: 30), with a productivity (PAY) of 7.47 and citation score (CAY) of 141.93 in each active year. Articles in this cluster have appeared since 1987, but publications have shown major increases since 2000. Approximately 44% of the cluster’s articles were published in the most recent period (2015–2019). Thus, knowledge management and innovation are highly discussed topics for the current times. Researchers could find new avenues to explore in this domain. Knowledge management and innovation cover a wide range of topics and new developments. The major topics include ‘knowledge transfer,’ ‘tactic knowledge,’ ‘knowledge marketing,’ ‘knowledge sharing,’ ‘knowledge dissemination,’ ‘adoptive capacity,’ ‘strategic orientation,’ ‘company experience,’ ‘innovation,’ ‘product innovation capability,’ ‘CRM 2.0’ and ‘artificial intelligence.’ The most influential works of the cluster are those of Cavusgil et al. (2003), Lapierre (2000) and Peters (2010).

Cluster 5 is the smallest cluster, with 157 articles related to sales and salesperson. The cluster has 144 publications cited with 2,292 citations (NCP: 144, TC: 2,292). Despite being the smallest cluster, the cluster has published in 32 of JBIM’s 34 years (NAY: 32). The cluster also shows the lowest citations per publication (C/P) of 14.60 and citations per active year (CAY) of 71.63. The cluster began in the inception period of the journal (1986–1990) and has had a steady growth during the seven identified periods. It could be inferred that, unlike the other clusters, Cluster 5 has had a slow growth rate over the years. Thus, the journal could consider encouraging further research on this theme. The major themes discussed in this cluster include ‘salesperson performance,’ ‘buyer–salesperson relationship,’ ‘sales orientation–customer orientation (SOCO),’ ‘salesperson–customer interactions,’ ‘salesperson customer orientation,’ ‘sales presentation skills,’ ‘salesperson job satisfaction,’ ‘salesperson role stress,’ ‘salesperson behavior,’ ‘manager performance’ and ‘channel partner performance.’ The most cited works in this cluster are those of Lund (2003), Keilloret al.(2000) and Boleset al.(1997).
